body:
From caste discrimination to organized demands for rights

Dr. Bhimrao Ramji Ambedkar (1891–1956) was an important leader of movements against untouchability and caste discrimination. Born into a Mahar family, he experienced restrictions associated with untouchability during his childhood and education.

Ambedkar argued that ending caste discrimination required more than moral appeals. Oppressed communities needed education, organization, enforceable civil rights and political representation.

His approach connected social equality with access to public institutions and participation in decisions made by the state.

Organizations and public communication

Ambedkar used writing and public organization to explain the injustices experienced by communities then commonly called the Depressed Classes.

He was associated with the Marathi periodical Mooknayak, begun in 1920, and established the Bahishkrit Hitakarini Sabha in 1924. The Sabha promoted education and the advancement of socially excluded communities.

These activities helped turn individual experiences of discrimination into collective demands.

Mahad Satyagraha, 1927: Access to public water

At Mahad in Maharashtra, people treated as untouchable were prevented from using the Chavdar public water tank, despite measures intended to make public facilities accessible.

On 20 March 1927, Ambedkar led participants in asserting their right to obtain water from the tank. The purpose was not simply to satisfy the immediate need for drinking water. It was to demonstrate that access to public resources should not depend on caste.

Mahad Satyagraha, 1927: Assertion of the right to use the Chavdar public water tank. It was a civil-rights struggle against untouchability.

Kalaram Temple Satyagraha, 1930: Temple entry

Ambedkar also challenged restrictions on religious entry. The Kalaram Temple Satyagraha began in 1930 at Nashik in Maharashtra. It asserted the right of people excluded by caste to enter the temple.

The two movements are often confused because both challenged untouchability, but their immediate demands were different.

MovementPlace and yearImmediate demand
Mahad SatyagrahaMahad, 1927Access to the Chavdar public water tank
Kalaram Temple SatyagrahaNashik, 1930Entry into the Kalaram temple

Political representation and the Poona Pact

Ambedkar also sought political safeguards for communities that had long been excluded from positions of power.

In 1932, the British Communal Award proposed separate electorates for the Depressed Classes. Under a separate electorate, voters belonging to a specified community elect representatives through a separate electoral arrangement for that community.

Mahatma Gandhi opposed separate electorates for the Depressed Classes. Following negotiations, the Poona Pact was agreed on 24 September 1932.

The pact substituted reserved seats within joint electorates for the proposed separate electorates. In a joint electorate, eligible voters vote together rather than being divided into separate electorates by community. Under the pact, a preliminary election by Depressed Class voters was also provided to select a panel of candidates for the reserved seats.

The pact increased the number of reserved seats for the Depressed Classes in provincial legislatures from 71 to 148.

Separate electorate and reserved seat in a joint electorate are different arrangements. A reserved seat identifies the category of representative, while a joint electorate retains a common electorate for the final election.

From social protest to constitutional equality

Ambedkar later served as the Chairman of the Drafting Committee of the Constituent Assembly. The Constitution adopted important safeguards against discrimination.

Article 17 abolished untouchability and prohibited its practice in any form. The enforcement of any disability arising from untouchability is an offence punishable in accordance with law.

Article 15(1) prohibits the state from discriminating against citizens only on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth. Article 15(2) also prohibits specified restrictions on access to shops, public restaurants, hotels and places of public entertainment, and on the use of wells, tanks, bathing ghats, roads and places of public resort maintained wholly or partly out of State funds or dedicated to public use, on those grounds.

These provisions reflect the importance of equality and public access in the wider struggle against caste discrimination.

Prelims focus

  • 1920: Mooknayak periodical associated with Ambedkar.
  • 1924: Bahishkrit Hitakarini Sabha.
  • 20 March 1927: Mahad Satyagraha for access to the Chavdar water tank.
  • 1930: Kalaram Temple Satyagraha at Nashik.
  • 24 September 1932: Poona Pact; reserved provincial seats increased from 71 to 148.
  • Trap: Mahad concerned public water access; Kalaram concerned temple entry.

[NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, 2020–21, Chapter 8, printed pp. 101 and 103–105; Supreme Court of India, Centenary of Dr. B.R. Ambedkar's Enrolment as an Advocate, Mahad Satyagraha, sections on the legal background and the march of 20 March 1927, consulted 20 November 2026; Ministry of External Affairs, Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches, Volume 10, note on the Poona Pact and its provincial seat provisions, consulted 20 November 2026; NCERT, Social and Political Life–III, Class 8, 2018–19, Chapter 8, Confronting Marginalisation, printed pp. 94–96.]

pictures.caption: Mahad and Kalaram addressed different forms of exclusion from public and religious spaces.

title: B.R. Ambedkar: Civil Rights, Public Access and Political Representation

body:
One goal, several approaches

The movements associated with Phule, Narayana Guru, Periyar and Ambedkar all challenged caste-based inequality, but they did not use identical methods.

Their distinctive approaches are important because an objective question may describe an idea or institution without naming its leader. Identifying the method often helps identify the reformer.

ReformerPrincipal regionCharacteristic approach
Jyotirao PhuleMaharashtraEducation and organized challenge to caste superiority through Satyashodhak Samaj
Narayana GuruKeralaSpiritual equality, educational uplift and SNDP Yogam
PeriyarTamil regionRationalism, Self-Respect Movement and reform of marriage customs
B.R. AmbedkarWestern India and all-India politicsPublic access, civil rights, organization and political representation

Social equality was not limited to a single form

Educational equality meant opening learning opportunities to people previously excluded. Religious and social equality included challenges to exclusion from temples and public spaces. Political equality required a meaningful voice in decisions affecting a community.

These goals reinforced one another. Education could support organization, while organization could turn demands for equal treatment into public campaigns.

Gujarat connection: Ambedkar and Baroda

A significant connection with present-day Gujarat concerns Baroda State.

In 1913, Ambedkar received a scholarship from Maharaja Sayajirao Gaekwad III of Baroda for higher education at Columbia University in New York.

This support was important in Ambedkar's educational development. His later experiences of caste discrimination, including during his association with Baroda, also demonstrated that educational qualifications did not automatically remove social prejudice.

Gujarat connection: Sayajirao Gaekwad III of Baroda supported Ambedkar's higher education through a scholarship in 1913.

Other early movements of social assertion

Anti-caste assertion was not restricted to the 4 principal leaders discussed here. For example, Ghasidas was associated with the Satnami movement in Central India, which worked among marginalized communities and challenged inequalities in social status.

Such movements illustrate a broader historical change: communities facing discrimination increasingly developed their own institutions, leaders and forms of collective action.

Distinguishing the institutions

  • Satyashodhak Samaj, 1873: Jyotirao Phule; Maharashtra.
  • SNDP Yogam, 1903: Narayana Guru and his associates; Kerala.
  • Self-Respect Movement, 1925: Periyar; Tamil region.
  • Bahishkrit Hitakarini Sabha, 1924: Ambedkar; advancement of socially excluded communities.

Do not treat the word reform as meaning only religious reform. Some movements used spiritual teaching, while others emphasized rationalism, public rights, education or political representation.

Prelims focus

  • Phule: Satyashodhak Samaj and education.
  • Narayana Guru: Spiritual equality and SNDP Yogam.
  • Periyar: Rationalism and Self-Respect Movement.
  • Ambedkar: Public rights and political representation.
  • 1913: Sayajirao Gaekwad III of Baroda provided Ambedkar a scholarship for higher education.
  • Trap: Satyashodhak Samaj and SNDP Yogam were founded in different regions and in different years.

[NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, 2020–21, Chapter 8, printed pp. 102–105; Supreme Court of India, Centenary of Dr. B.R. Ambedkar's Enrolment as an Advocate, biographical section on the 1913 Baroda scholarship, consulted 20 November 2026; Kerala Tourism, Formation of SNDP Yogam, consulted 20 November 2026; Tamil Nadu History Congress, The Self-Respect Movement of Periyar, consulted 20 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Four reformers are linked to their distinctive methods, institutions and years, with all four connected to opposition to caste-based inequality.
pictures.caption: Four reform traditions connected dignity with different means of achieving equality.

title: Comparing Anti-Caste Reformers and Understanding Their Gujarat Connections

body:
Widowhood and unequal social treatment

In several communities during the 19th century, widows faced severe social restrictions. They might be discouraged or prohibited from remarrying, excluded from celebrations, restricted in their appearance or dependent on relatives for economic support.

Some widows also faced difficulties concerning property and maintenance. These conditions made widowhood both a social and an economic issue.

Two major reform campaigns addressed different aspects of this problem: opposition to sati and support for widow remarriage.

Raja Rammohun Roy and the abolition of sati

Sati referred to the burning of a widow on her deceased husband's funeral pyre. The practice existed in some regions and communities; it should not be described as a practice followed by all Hindu widows.

Raja Rammohun Roy campaigned against sati. He criticized the practice and argued that its supposed religious justification was mistaken. He used writings and discussion to support his position.

In 1829, Lord William Bentinck enacted Bengal Sati Regulation XVII, which declared the practice illegal within the territory to which the regulation applied.

The regulation is an important milestone in the legal prohibition of sati. It was initially a Bengal Presidency measure; its enactment should not be interpreted as every part of the subcontinent becoming subject to the identical regulation on the same day.

1829: Bengal Sati Regulation XVII, enacted under Lord William Bentinck. Raja Rammohun Roy was an important campaigner against the practice.

Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar and widow remarriage

Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar worked for the recognition of widow remarriage. He used his knowledge of Sanskrit texts to argue that the remarriage of Hindu widows could be justified and should not be treated as inherently unacceptable.

The Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act, 1856, also known as Act XV of 1856, legally recognized the remarriage of Hindu widows. It also provided that children of such marriages were not to be considered illegitimate merely because their mother had previously been married.

However, the law did not establish complete equality in inheritance. Under its original provisions, specified interests that a widow held in her deceased husband's property could cease on her remarriage.

This distinction matters: permission to remarry and equal property rights were separate questions.

Widow-remarriage campaigns beyond Bengal

The campaign spread to several parts of India.

  • Kandukuri Veeresalingam Pantulu: Promoted widow remarriage in the Telugu-speaking region of the Madras Presidency.
  • Swami Dayanand Saraswati: Supported widow remarriage through the reform outlook associated with the Arya Samaj, founded in 1875.
  • Reformers in Bombay: Also worked to encourage widow remarriage.

Despite legal change and organized campaigning, many remarried widows continued to encounter social opposition. The existence of a law did not by itself guarantee widespread acceptance.

How the two legal changes differed

YearMeasureImmediate purpose
1829Bengal Sati Regulation XVIIProhibition of sati in the regulation's territory
1856Hindu Widows' Remarriage ActLegal recognition of Hindu widow remarriage

Prelims focus

  • Raja Rammohun Roy: Major campaigner against sati.
  • 1829: Bengal Sati Regulation XVII under Lord William Bentinck.
  • Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar: Major supporter of widow remarriage.
  • 1856: Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act.
  • Veeresalingam: Widow-remarriage reform in the Telugu-speaking region.
  • Trap: The 1829 measure concerned sati; the 1856 measure concerned widow remarriage.

[NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, 2020–21, Chapter 8, Women, Caste and Reform, printed pp. 94–97; Bengal Sati Regulation XVII of 1829, sections 1–2, historical statutory text, consulted 20 November 2026; Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act, 1856, sections 1–2 and 5, historical statutory text, consulted 20 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: The 1829 sati prohibition under Bentinck, supported by Rammohun Roy, contrasts with the 1856 recognition of widow remarriage supported by Vidyasagar.
pictures.caption: Abolishing sati and permitting widow remarriage were two distinct legal reforms.

title: The Campaigns against Sati and Restrictions on Widow Remarriage
